For Israel, the promises of numerous offspring symbolize the fulfillment of covenants and the victory of God's people. It is also a call to see in each new generation a manifestation of God's faithfulness and creative power.

sens: Vehicle or stretcher for transporting a person
Covered cart or chariot
Luxuriously appointed means of transport
H6632A.detail:
1. A litter is a vehicle designed to carry a person, particularly someone of high rank or ill, as found in many ancient cultures. It is a stretcher or a litter, often carried by men or drawn by animals. The litter offers the traveler a reclining or semi-reclining position, protected and comfortable.
2. In the biblical context, the litter specifically refers to a chariot or a covered vehicle used for prestigious travel. At the offerings of the Tabernacle, the princes of Israel bring litters: "They brought their offering before the Lord: six covered wagons" (Numbers 7:3).
3. The word also describes a means of transport intended for long journeys, combining utility and dignity. In the prophecy of Isaiah, the Lord announces the return of the exiles: "They will bring all your brothers from among all the nations, as an offering to the Lord, on horses, in chariots and litters, on mules and camels" (Isaiah 66:20).
H6632A.origine: The Hebrew word צָב (tsav) literally means a container or a vehicle for transport. It comes from the root צוב (tsuv), which evokes the idea of loading or carrying. In biblical Hebrew, the term applies to any means of conveyance arranged for comfortable or majestic transport, particularly in contexts of worship or official travel.
H6632A.emploi: The word צָב appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in solemn contexts: in Numbers 7:3, during the dedication of the Tabernacle, and in Isaiah 66:20, in a vision of messianic restoration. In both cases, the litter symbolizes an honorable means of transport suitable for the solemnity of the moment. The context of the offerings at the Tabernacle and the gathering of the exiles shows that this vehicle holds particular cultic and spiritual significance.
H6632A.portee: The litter reminds us that the dignity of transport in Scripture is linked to the honor of the one traveling. Its appearance at key moments of worship and covenant underscores the importance of every moment dedicated to the Lord. For the Christian reader, it is an image of the care with which God surrounds His people in His great movements of grace and restoration.

sens: A small animal that crawls on the ground, with an elongated body and scales
An unclean animal according to the law of Moses
H6632B.detail:
1. The lizard is a small reptile that moves by crawling on the ground. It is an elongated animal covered in scales. In Leviticus 11:29, it appears in the list of animals that crawl on the ground, like the mole and the mouse.
2. According to the law given to Moses, the lizard is declared unclean and must not be eaten. This prohibition is part of the dietary laws that distinguish the Israelites by separating them from other peoples.
H6632B.origine: The Hebrew word צָב (tsav) designates a crawling reptile. Its initial image is that of an animal that drags itself on the ground. The exact nature of the creature in question is not entirely certain: some believe it to be a type of tortoise, others a now-extinct animal or a species unknown today. The word appears only in the purity lists of the Law.
H6632B.emploi: The word צָב (tsav) appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 11:29, in the list of unclean animals that crawl on the ground. It is listed alongside other minor creatures like the mole and the mouse. This unique mention shows that the animal was known to the Israelites of the time, enough to be specifically prohibited as food. The context is purely legal: it serves to mark a religious and cultural distinction between what is clean and what is unclean.
H6632B.portee: This mention of the lizard among unclean animals reminds us that the law of Moses encompassed even small creatures and the details of daily life. It shows that holiness in the Old Testament is also manifested through simple and repeated actions: knowing what one can or cannot eat. For the Christian reader, this list is a testament to the rigor with which God guided His people and the break it represents in the New Testament, where Jesus declares all foods clean.

sens: Make war, engage in combat
Present oneself for military service, be mobilized
Serve at the sacred tent or temple
H6633.detail:
1. To make war, engage in combat: this is the action of going into battle, of fighting. The word evokes the image of a troop gathering and marching to meet the enemy. "The nations that will come to attack the mountain of Zion" (Isaiah 29:8) illustrates this sense of an organized attack.
2. To present oneself for military service, to be mobilized: this refers to the action of enlisting or being enlisted in an army, transitioning from civilian to soldier ready to depart. "The secretary of the army chief who was responsible for enrolling the people of the land" (2 Kings 25:19) illustrates this conscription process.
3. To serve at the sacred tent or temple: by extension, the word designates any structured and disciplined service, particularly the religious ministry at the tabernacle. "From the age of twenty-five years and older, every Levite shall enter the service of the tent of meeting to perform a function" (Numbers 8:24) shows this shift from military to sacred: a Levite "fights" for God by serving at the tabernacle with the same rigor as a soldier.
H6633.origine: The Hebrew verb צָבָא (tsava) fundamentally means "to go forward, to arrange in order." It is related to the noun צְבָאוֹת (tsevaot), "armies," which appears constantly in the expression "the Lord of hosts" (Lord Sabaoth). The initial image is that of an organized troop, military or religious, moving with order and discipline. The word evokes structure, hierarchy, and obedience: one who fights or serves in an army must follow ranks and commands.
H6633.emploi: The verb צָבָא appears twelve times in the provided usages, primarily in military and religious contexts. In the Old Testament, it first designates the act of "fighting" or "going to war": it is the action of the armies of Israel preparing for battle (Numbers 31:7, Isaiah 29:8). It also means "to enlist" or "to mobilize": the process by which an army is formed by gathering able men (2 Kings 25:19, Jeremiah 52:25). The word then transitions to the religious domain: "to perform a function" at the tent of meeting (Numbers 8:24) or "to assemble" (Exodus 38:8) women for the service of the tabernacle. This extension of meaning shows that for Israel, serving God was conceived as an orderly army, with its posts, ages of entry, and strict organization.
H6633.portee: This word reveals how the Bible views the service of God: not as a relaxed or optional activity, but as a fight and a disciplined commitment, requiring order and totality of self. Those who serve the God of Israel are fighters for His cause, mobilized and enlisted for a mission that transcends their own interest. This image invites the believer to consider their Christian life not as a peaceful routine, but as an active and structured mobilization.

sens: To desire, to want something
To be willing to, to consent to
To sovereignly will, to decide (especially for God)
H6634.detail:
1. To desire or want something: this is to experience a natural inclination towards what one wishes. In Daniel 5:19, King Nebuchadnezzar "killed those whom he wanted," showing his personal desire to exercise this power.

2. To be willing to, to consent to, to give one's agreement: the idea of a will that accepts or refuses. The word here expresses a good disposition, a heart acceptance.

3. To sovereignly will, to decide without obstacle (notably for God): this is the all-powerful will that operates without any resistance. In Daniel 4:17 and 4:35, it is said that God "gives it to whom he pleases," expressing that his will is accomplished without restriction: he reigns over kingdoms and raises or lowers them according to his sole decision.
H6634.origine: This Aramaic word comes from a root expressing the idea of leaning towards, being inclined. It is related to the corresponding Hebrew verb and evokes an inclination of the heart or will. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the biblical idea that divine will needs no permission: it accomplishes itself.
H6634.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in biblical Aramaic, only in the book of Daniel (chapters 4, 5, and 7), a book written partly in the language of the Babylonian empire. It is used almost exclusively to express the sovereign will of God or a powerful king who disposes of men and kingdoms without restriction. In Daniel 4:17, 4:25, 4:32, and 4:35, it always refers to the divine will to give power to whom it wants. In Daniel 5:19, it is King Nebuchadnezzar who uses it to describe his own power of life and death. The fundamental meaning remains constant: a will that operates freely, without being hindered.
H6634.portee: This word reveals that God never acts by constraint or obligation: his reign is based on his sovereign and free will. For the believer, this reassures: God suffers no opposition; he distributes kingdoms and takes them away according to his wisdom, far beyond our human calculations. Recognizing that God acts "as he pleases" invites us to trust him, even when the events of the world perplex us.

sens: Organized group of soldiers in battle order
Troop of warriors on campaign
Organized multitude of celestial beings
The stars (sun, moon, stars) considered collectively
Military service, action of waging war
Collection of created things, ordered totality
H6635A.detail:
1. The army of Israel is primarily an organized and counted military force: in the desert, Moses counts those who are "able to go to war" (Numbers 1:3), and each tribe must provide its "army corps" of so many thousands of men (Numbers 2:19).
2. On campaign, the army moves: it is a troop that "goes out" to fight, under the command of a general like Joab (2 Samuel 8:16).
3. The word expands to celestial creatures: in Nehemiah 9:6, the "host of heaven" refers to the angels who "bow down" before God.
4. It also applies to the stars—the sun, the moon, the stars—that God created and which "serve" their Creator in a sense (2 Kings 23:4 speaks of the "host of heaven" to burn).
5. The word also evokes military service itself, the action of going to war as a duty and service to the king or God.
6. Finally, in Genesis 2:1, "all the host of heaven and earth" refers to the order of creation as a whole, the cosmos harmoniously organized.
H6635A.origine: The Hebrew word צָבָא comes from a root that evokes the idea of "going out," "forming ranks," "organizing in formation." That is why it primarily designates an organized troop ready for action. The word can apply to any ordered multitude that "goes out" or "presents itself"—soldiers in battle, angels in procession, the stars in the sky. This root reflects the biblical idea that everything that exists, from the humblest to the greatest, is organized under God's order.
H6635A.emploi: The word appears 136 times in the Bible, mainly in historical books and legislative texts. Its most frequent use is military: the book of Numbers enumerates the contingents (about 130 times), and the books of Samuel-Kings speak of the generals who "command" it. The same word also designates the divine crowds—angels and stars—that serve God, as in Nehemiah 9:6. This extension of meaning reveals a biblical theology: from soldier to servant of divine order, everything that is well organized in creation is an "army" under the direction of the Lord. In Deuteronomy 4:19 and 2 Kings 23:4, the "host of heaven" also reminds that even the stars, which the pagans worshipped, belong to God.
H6635A.portee: This word teaches that order in creation—military, celestial, or cosmic—is not random: it is God's "army," ordered and commanded by him. For the believer, this means that God masters the powers of the world, military forces, the stars, and even celestial spirits. In times of threat or weakness, knowing that everything obeys God in an "organized army" can strengthen trust in his omnipotence and wisdom.

sens: The Lord who commands all the armies of heaven and earth
God in his omnipotence and absolute sovereignty
The Lord recognized as heavenly King and judge of nations
H6635B.detail:
1. The Lord who commands all the armies of heaven and earth—"hosts" refers to the multitudes of celestial creatures (angels) and earthly beings, visible and invisible, that God directs. This title emphasizes that the Lord does not dominate just one people or region, but the entire universe. In 1 Samuel 1:3, Eli receives Hannah who prays to "the Lord of hosts": she addresses the God whose power extends beyond the mere temple.
2. God in his omnipotence and absolute sovereignty—This title expresses that nothing escapes the control and plan of the Lord. The prophets use it to remind Israel and the nations that God accomplishes his intentions despite human powers. In Isaiah 5:7, "the Lord of hosts" has planted his vineyard (Israel); in Isaiah 1:24, he announces that he will surely take vengeance on his enemies.
3. The Lord recognized as heavenly King and judge of nations—In the Psalms (24:10, 46:8), this title celebrates the God who reigns above all creation and who intervenes on behalf of his people. It assures believers that despite earthly threats, their invisible King possesses incomparable authority.
H6635B.origine: The Hebrew word צָבָא (tsava) literally means "army" or "troop." The Bible uses this term to refer not only to human armies but also to celestial bodies (the stars, called "hosts of heaven"), angels, and ultimately the entire created universe. By joining this name to that of the Lord (YHWH), the title "Lord of hosts" means that God is the supreme Commander of all these forces. This title appears more than 270 times in the Old Testament, especially among the prophets.
H6635B.emploi: The title "the Lord of hosts" appears 274 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in the books of Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Psalms, and the Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah notably). It emerges forcefully when the Bible wants to emphasize that God acts with all his sovereign power. In 1 Samuel 4:4, the Israelites invoke "the Lord of hosts sitting on the cherubim" at the moment of a battle lost in advance, affirming their confidence in God's invisible power. The prophets use it to announce certain judgments: in Isaiah 1:24 and 5:9, this title precedes words of condemnation against sin. In the Psalms, it assures the people that their invisible King remains stronger than all earthly enemies (Psalms 46:8).
H6635B.portee: This title reminds the believer that God depends on no one and fears no power—human, political, military, or even celestial—because he commands them all. For someone overwhelmed by circumstances or threatened by forces that seem invincible, invoking "the Lord of hosts" is an act of faith that restores perspective: he who reigns over the invisible also reigns over the visible. This comforts and strengthens the believer in trial.

sens: A group of soldiers organized for combat
Troop, band of warriors on the march or mobilized
Organized multitude (angels, stars, creation)
Military service, obligation to bear arms
War, combat, armed conflict
Military expedition, campaign
H6635H.detail:
1. An army is a group of soldiers trained and equipped to wage war. They fight together under a single command. In Numbers 1:3, all men "able to bear arms" are counted, meaning those capable of serving as soldiers.
2. The term also refers to a troop on the march or an armed contingent sent for a specific mission. In Numbers 31:6, Moses "sent to the army these thousand men by tribe" with their leaders to execute a judgment of God.
3. The Bible broadens this term to encompass any organized multitude: angels are called "the army of heaven," the sun and moon are the "host of heaven," images of the order and power of creation (Isaiah 40:2 refers to "the army of the Lord").
4. Bearing arms means having the status and duty of military service: being of age and condition to go to war. It is a responsibility of a fighting citizen in service to their people.
5. The term also signifies war itself, the armed conflict between peoples. In Joshua 22:33, the tribes decide not to go "armed" to ravage the land of the sons of Reuben and Gad — it is the threat of combat that is dismissed.
6. An army can also be a campaign, an organized military operation. In 1 Chronicles 20:1, David sends "his army" — a directed force for conquest.
H6635H.origine: The Hebrew word צָבָא (tsa.va) comes from a root that expresses the idea of "going out," "rising up," "going into battle." It refers to what "goes out" or "marches" — hence the meaning of a troop in action. The word appears 41 times in the Old Testament, mainly in war narratives and military counts in the book of Numbers. It also encompasses the biblical image of the "hosts of heaven" (angels, stars), showing that even the celestial order is conceived as an organized and powerful reality, subject to God.
H6635H.emploi: The word צָבָא appears 41 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the books of the Law (Numbers), history (Joshua, Samuel, Chronicles), and the prophets (Isaiah, Daniel). It is very frequent in the military counts of Numbers, where men "able to bear arms" are counted (all occurrences in Numbers 1 and 26). It often signifies the organized army of Israel or neighboring nations (1 Samuel 28:1), and can designate a troop sent on a specific mission, as in Numbers 31:6. The term also expands to broader meanings: the "hosts of heaven" (Isaiah 40:2), which represent cosmic order and power, or military service as an obligation (2 Chronicles 26:11 mentions Uzziah organizing his army). The term can also refer to "war" itself (Joshua 22:33), designating the feared or engaged armed conflict.
H6635H.portee: Understanding that the term "army" encompasses both the practical reality of combat and military service, and the biblical vision of an ordered, powerful universe, obedient to God. It reminds the reader that brute force — whether military or cosmic — is never autonomous: it is subject to the judgment and will of the Lord. The mention of the "hosts of heaven" (Isaiah 40:2) invites us to see all authority and power as submitted to God, a comfort for the believer in the face of earthly powers.

sens: organized group of soldiers intended for war
military campaign, armed expedition
function, charge, work assigned to someone
activity, occupation
H6635I.detail:
1. The term primarily designates a constituted army, an organized group of warriors: in Numbers 31:14, Moses becomes angry with "the commanders of the army" who return from an expedition.
2. It can also refer to the campaign itself, the military action: the "expedition" of Numbers 31:14 is the result of what these armies have accomplished.
3. The meaning broadens to encompass any function or charge assigned to someone: in Numbers 4:3, the Levites "fit to perform any service in the tent of meeting" are those capable of fulfilling the service of the sanctuary, akin to organized military work.
4. By extension, it refers to ordinary activity, the work or occupation to which each is assigned: in Job 7:1, the text speaks of "the life of man on earth" as a kind of service or task, a continual activity.
H6635I.origine: The Hebrew word צָבָא comes from a root that evokes the idea of "going out, rising up in order." The basic image is that of a troop going out to battle or to work in an organized manner. The word retains this sense of organization and direction: this is why it applies to both an army and a cultic service or an assigned task. The root suggests the movement of those who rise together for a mission.
H6635I.emploi: This word appears thirteen times in the provided references, primarily in the books of Numbers and Chronicles. In chapters 4 and 8 of Numbers, it designates the "service" that the Levites must fulfill at the tabernacle from a certain age: it is an organized work, like that of a troop. In Numbers 31:14, it refers to the "army" returning from the expedition against Midian. In 1 Chronicles 25:1, David entrusts musicians with the service of worship, this service being described with the same solemnity as a military charge. The term gradually shifts from a warrior meaning to that of a simple function or assigned work, as in Job 7:1 where human life itself is a kind of incessant service.
H6635I.portee: This word enriches the understanding of what the Bible calls true "service" to God or to the community. It shows that fulfilling a function, whether priestly, cultic, or ordinary, is a serious and organized reality, comparable to the order of an army. For the believer, it reminds us that the Christian life requires the same discipline and commitment as that of a warrior: there is a "good soldier" in the service of God (see 2 Timothy 2:3-4).

sens: City in the plain of the Jordan, one of the five cities destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah
Symbol of divine destruction and the anger of the Lord
H6636.detail:
1. Tseboïm is an ancient city located in the plain of the Jordan, mentioned among the five great cities of the region, alongside Sodom and Gomorrah. It had its own king and participated in military alliances (Genesis 14:2, 8). Like Sodom and Gomorrah, it was destroyed by the Lord due to its sins (Deuteronomy 29:23).

2. In the Bible, Tseboïm represents the classic example of divine judgment: it is cited alongside Sodom and Gomorrah to remind the Israelites of what happens to cities that rebel against God. The prophet Hosea invokes it to show Israel the gravity of what it risks if it persists in unfaithfulness (Hosea 11:8).
H6636.origine: The name Tseboïm means "gazelles" in Hebrew, derived from the root צבי (tsévi). This name, given to a city, may evoke the nature of the site or a geographical feature. It is a typical geographical proper name of the ancient Levant, where places bore names of remarkable animals or plants.
H6636.emploi: Tseboïm appears five times in the Bible, always in connection with Sodom and Gomorrah and the five cities of the plain of the Jordan. It is first mentioned as one of the Canaanite cities (Genesis 10:19), then in the account of the war against the kings of the Jordan (Genesis 14:2, 8), where it figures alongside its allies. Two major passages make it a symbol: Deuteronomy 29:23 mentions it to describe the ruins and desolation caused by the anger of the Lord, and Hosea 11:8 uses it to warn Israel of the fate that awaits it if it betrays its God. The usage is consistent: Tseboïm always represents a case of destruction and judgment.
H6636.portee: Tseboïm reminds the reader that divine judgment on sin is real and radical: an entire city can be wiped out. It invites a fear of God and vigilance against idolatry and unfaithfulness. Its mention in prophetic warnings shows that God never abandons His people without first warning them, offering them a choice: one need only contemplate the fate of Tseboïm to understand the consequences of rebellion.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
H6637.detail: Hatsobéba is a minor character in the Old Testament, mentioned only once in the genealogy of Judah. He is the son of Kots and the brother of Anub and Harum (1 Chronicles 4:8). His name literally means "the slow one" or "the one who lingers," an evocative image, although Scripture tells us nothing of his life or deeds. He represents a lineage of the tribe of Judah at a time when the kingdom was divided between Judah and Israel.
H6637.origine: The name Hatsobéba comes from a Hebrew root that evokes slowness or lingering. The genealogy in which he appears dates back to the time of the divided monarchy, a period in Israel's history (around the 9th-8th century BCE) when the unified kingdom established by David had split into two rival kingdoms.
H6637.emploi: Hatsobéba appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:8, in the midst of a genealogical list of the tribe of Judah. He is presented as the son of Kots and the brother of two other men, Anub and Harum, in a enumeration that lists the descendants of this Judean lineage. These genealogies in the book of Chronicles, although they do not recount any particular exploits, attest to the existence of important families and clans within the people of God at different periods of its history.

sens: To swell, to increase in volume
To distend (the belly)
H6638.detail: 1. To swell simply means to increase in volume, to inflate. It is a physical action where a part of the body swells with water or air. 2. In the two biblical usages provided, this verb precisely describes the belly of a woman swelling: in Numbers 5:22 and 5:27, it is the miraculous sign of divine judgment on a woman who may have committed adultery. Her belly swells as a visible manifestation of guilt, while her thigh withers — two opposing signs that mark the entire body.
H6638.origine: The Hebrew verb צָבָה (tsavah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of swelling or distension. The word literally describes what fills up, what takes on volume. It is a simple and concrete verb, with few derivatives in the Bible.
H6638.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Old Testament, and both occurrences are found exactly in the same passage: the rite of divine judgment in Numbers 5:22-27. This text describes the judgment of a woman suspected of marital infidelity: she drinks a bitter water, and if she is guilty, the water produces a double effect on her body — her belly swells and her thigh withers. The use of the same verb in both verses shows that the swelling of the belly is the key sign of miraculous judgment.
H6638.portee: This word reminds us that God knows the secrets and hidden faults, and that He acts to reveal the truth. The swelling of the belly, far from being a simple medical description, symbolizes the judgment made visible, the public shame of one who has violated the marriage covenant. It is a call to purity and faithfulness in married life.

sens: To swell, to increase in volume
To fill with a substance (liquid or air) that distends the tissues
To become tumescent, to swell (referring to the belly or a part of the body)
H6639.detail:
1. The verb expresses the physical action of swelling or increasing in volume. In Numbers 5:21, in the context of the curse sworn against the woman suspected of infidelity, "to swell" her belly refers to pathological swelling, the abdominal distension that results from divine curse — a visible and corporeal manifestation of judgment.
2. The underlying image is that of internal accumulation that causes the organ to lose its normal shape, creating a swollen and monstrous appearance.
3. In this passage, the swelling of the belly functions as a public and undeniable sign of guilt: an unfaithful woman cannot hide it.
H6639.origine: The Hebrew root צָבַה (tsavah) refers to the idea of filling and swelling. The word belongs to the semantic field of visible physical transformations of the body. Its usage here, combined with the "withering" of the thigh, creates a contrast: while one part of the body will become emaciated, the other will swell, making the judgment manifest and irreversible.
H6639.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Numbers 5:21). It is found in the passage concerning the trial of the woman suspected of infidelity (the biblical ordeal). In this very specific legal and religious context, the swelling of the belly is one of the two bodily curses stated: it accompanies the withering of the thigh to signify that God visibly intervenes to reveal the truth. It is a judgment of the body, not just a moral sanction.
H6639.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, divine judgment can manifest through tangible physical signs. The swelling of the belly publicly denounces lies and infidelity, showing that God does not allow hidden sins to remain concealed. For the reader, this passage teaches that God sees all and that His justice is not hidden behind words: it marks the body itself. It is also an invitation to take seriously the oaths and covenant promises.

sens: Object, creature or concrete reality
Matter, issue or subject
What is desired or sought
Fact, circumstance or situation
H6640.detail:
1. The word primarily designates any concrete thing, any object or creature that exists: in Daniel 6:17, the king seals the pit "so that nothing would be changed," meaning that no external circumstance could alter Daniel's situation — the word encompasses all material realities that could intervene.
2. It can mean a matter, an issue, or a subject of concern: what is being talked about, what is being discussed, what occupies our minds.
3. The word can also refer to what is desired, coveted, or sought: something one wants to obtain, a goal one pursues.
4. More broadly, it expresses a fact, a circumstance, or a given situation: everything that exists and can be stated or considered.
H6640.origine: This word belongs to the Hebrew family of terms expressing existence and reality. Its root evokes the idea of what is established, fixed, or subsisting. In Hebrew, it fits into the fundamental vocabulary that allows one to speak of everything that is — from material things to immaterial facts. The context of Daniel 6:17 shows the usage in a broad sense: the thing is everything that could change or be modified.
H6640.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 6:17, where it is translated as "nothing" in the sense of "no thing." The context is that of the story of Daniel in the lion's den: King Darius wants to ensure that no external intervention will alter Daniel's situation during the night. The word, negated by the particle of negation, thus means "no reality, no thing" can be changed — it expresses the total absence of possibility for modification, the irreversibility of what has been decided. This unique usage shows it in a solemn and judicial context.
H6640.portee: This word reminds us that God controls all things — even when everything seems sealed by the will of men and the laws of the kingdom. In the story of Daniel, the sealing of the pit by the rings of the nobles can do nothing against the power of the living God. For the reader, it is an invitation to recognize that God surpasses all material and human obstacles.

sens: Wild animal with spotted fur, scavenger
H6641.detail: 1. The hyena is a carnivorous animal known for its mixed-colored fur and scavenging behavior: it feeds on the remains left by other predators. The Hebrew word emphasizes this mixture of colors, the spots that mark its coat. In Jeremiah 12:9, God compares the unfaithful heritage of Israel to a "bird of prey" (or a hyena according to some ancient translations): a devastated possession, now prey to the vultures and wild beasts that come from all sides to devour it.
H6641.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be spotted, varied in colors." This image of mixed fur characterizes the hyena in the eyes of the ancient Hebrews. The animal is well known in the Middle East, feared for its strength and its role as a scavenger in the desert.
H6641.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Jeremiah 12:9). It is used poetically and symbolically: God reproaches Israel for having betrayed its covenant and compares its once-protected heritage to a wild animal left at the mercy of all predators. The image evokes tearing, destruction, and abandonment of the people to the mercy of their enemies.
H6641.portee: This striking image reminds us that unfaithfulness to God exposes the people to destruction. It serves as a warning: one who abandons the divine covenant loses divine protection and becomes vulnerable. For the Christian reader, this illustrates the importance of remaining attached to God to preserve life and blessing.

sens: to extend, offer something to someone
to provide food to someone for nourishment
H6642.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to extend or present something to someone, offering it within their reach. It is a concrete gesture of hospitality and generosity.
2. In the context of Ruth 2:14, it means to give food: Boaz commands his servants to give Ruth roasted grain during the meal. This gift nourishes the young foreign and poor woman, showing the master's kindness towards her.
H6642.origine: The verb צָבַט (tsavat) comes from a root that evokes the idea of grasping or extending. It is infrequent in Hebrew and appears rarely in the Bible. The meaning of "to give" is naturally linked to the action of extending something to someone, as one would do with the hand.
H6642.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Ruth 2:14. Boaz uses it to describe the action of his servants who offer roasted grain to Ruth at mealtime. It is an act of mercy towards a poor foreigner. The word emphasizes the concrete and personal gesture of generosity: it is not merely an alms, but a true inclusion at the table of the harvesters.
H6642.portee: This moment reveals Boaz's just and generous character. By giving Ruth enough to eat, he honors God by welcoming the foreigner and the poor. For the reader, it shows that true piety is expressed through simple and kind acts towards those who are vulnerable.

sens: Physical brilliance, visible splendor of a thing or place
Adornment, clothing or ornament that beautifies
Glory, honor, prestige of a person or people
Excellence, what is remarkable or of first rank
H6643A.detail:
1. Physical brilliance: what strikes the eye with its splendor. In Isaiah 23:9, God humiliates "all that shines" — these magnificent cities whose brilliance was admired. It is the glorious appearance of a thing.
2. Adornment or ornament: what decorates and beautifies, such as a woman's clothing or jewelry. In Ezekiel 7:20, the people were "proud of their magnificent adornment" — these beautiful objects worn to appear splendid.
3. Glory and honor: fame, dignity, what makes a people or a king esteemed. In 2 Samuel 1:19, the "elite" of Israel — literally its beauty, its glory — fell in battle: these were its most remarkable men.
4. What is excellent or of first rank: Ezekiel calls the Holy Land the "ornament" of the country, making it precious and desirable above all. Daniel speaks of the land of Israel as the most "beautiful," the most coveted.
H6643A.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of shining, radiating. It is related to Hebrew words meaning "gazelle" — the quintessential animal symbolizing grace and elegance. Therefore, beauty primarily denotes what is visible, what amazes the eye. The word appears in many proper names and regularly describes the splendor of cities, lands, and people coveted by the powerful.
H6643A.emploi: The word appears 18 times, mostly in the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel). It designates either the visual beauty of an object or place (Ezekiel 25:9 for the cities of Moab) or the glory of a people or the prestige of a king (2 Samuel 1:19 for the warriors of Israel). In the prophets, this word often takes on a critical tone: external beauty becomes a motif of vanity (Ezekiel 7:20) or pride that God will humble (Isaiah 23:9). It is also what tempts and seduces — conquerors covet "beautiful" lands for their riches (Daniel 11:16, 11:41, 11:45).
H6643A.portee: This word reminds us that the beauty and splendor of the world are not stable — they pass and can become traps of vanity. For the believer, it invites one not to place trust in external brilliance, whether personal, material, or political. It is an invitation to seek beyond what shines at first glance, knowing that only God grants true and lasting glory.

sens: Wild animal with fine and light legs, resembling a deer
Creature symbolizing agility and speed
Poetic figure of grace and elegance
H6643B.detail:
1. The gazelle is a wild animal that the Bible classifies among the pure animals allowed for consumption (Deuteronomy 14:5). It resembles the deer and the doe, with very fine and light legs. It is game that could be hunted freely, unlike livestock subject to rules.
2. The gazelle is admired for its exceptional speed and agility. Asahel, a swift warrior, is compared to a "gazelle of the fields" (2 Samuel 2:18), and the valiant soldiers to "gazelles on the mountains" (1 Chronicles 12:8). This speed becomes the biblical symbol of one who escapes quickly (Proverbs 6:5).
3. In the love poetry of the Song of Songs, the gazelle embodies graceful and light beauty: it is implored not to awaken love prematurely (Song of Songs 2:7), and the lover becomes a "gazelle" or a "fawn of the does" to symbolize his lightness and grace (Song of Songs 2:17).
H6643B.origine: The Hebrew word צְבִי (tsévi) designates this animal by the image of its elegance and remarkable character. The word comes from a root that evokes beauty and adornment. The feminine form צְבִיָּה (tséviiah) also means "gazelle." This word remains common in modern Hebrew to refer to the gazelle, an emblematic animal of the Middle East.
H6643B.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in three contexts. First, it designates a pure animal allowed for consumption under the same conditions as game (Deuteronomy 12:15, 14:5, 15:22; 1 Kings 4:23): it is a delicate and luxurious food. Secondly, the Bible uses the gazelle to figure a lively and swift person, particularly in warrior or athletic comparisons (2 Samuel 2:18, 1 Chronicles 12:8, Proverbs 6:5). Finally, the Song of Songs uses it as a poetic metaphor for grace, lightness, and elegance in the context of love: it is a term of admiration (Song of Songs 2:7, 2:9, 2:17, 3:5, 8:14). Isaiah 13:14 also uses it to evoke rapid flight.
H6643B.portee: The gazelle reminds us that God has created creatures endowed with particular beauty and remarkable agility. It teaches the believer that speed and lightness are qualities to cultivate to escape from evil (Proverbs 6:5). In the poetry of the Song, it invites contemplation of delicate grace and living love with respect and patience, without forcing it before its time.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the divided monarchy
H6644.detail: Tsibja is a man belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, living during the time of the divided monarchy of Israel. He is the son of Shaharaim and his wife Hodesh. He is part of a large family that includes Jobab, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Sachia, Mirmah, Abitub, and Elpaal. He appears only once in the Scriptures, in the genealogy of Benjamin recorded in the book of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 8:9).
H6644.origine: The name Tsibja means "deer" or "gazelle" in Hebrew, likely evoking the agility or grace of the animal. It is a common descriptive name in the Old Testament, where parents gave their children names that reflected nature or a desired quality.
H6644.emploi: Tsibja is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:9, in a genealogy listing the descendants of Benjamin. He is presented as a son of Shaharaim and Hodesh, among his brothers. This unique genealogical mention places him among the ancestors of the people of Benjamin, without any other details of his life being reported.

sens: woman of Beersheba, wife of King Ahaziah of Judah
mother of King Joash of Judah
H6645.detail: Tsibja is a woman who lived during the time of the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah. She was from Beersheba and became the wife of King Ahaziah of Judah. She is best known as the mother of King Joash, who became king of Judah at the age of seven after his father's death (2 Kings 12:1). Her name means "gazelle" in Hebrew, evoking a graceful and agile creature.
H6645.origine: The name Tsibja comes from the Hebrew root meaning "gazelle" or "deer." It is an animal name that expresses grace and delicacy, quite common for women in the ancient Near East.
H6645.emploi: Tsibja is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both times to identify the mother of King Joash: once in 2 Kings 12:1 and once in 2 Chronicles 24:1, which report the same event. She plays no active role in the biblical narrative, but her presence simply marks the royal genealogy of Judah, establishing the link between her husband Ahaziah and her son Joash.

sens: four-legged animal, graceful and light, from the antelope family
symbol of grace and beauty in poetic language
H6646.detail:
1. The gazelle is a wild, slender, and elegant animal, known for its speed and agility. In the nature of the Middle East, where the biblical authors lived, it was an admired animal for its graceful appearance. The two gazelles or their fawns are compared to the breasts of the bride in the Song of Songs, evoking the delicate and harmonious beauty of the female body: "Your two breasts are like two fawns, like the twins of a gazelle" (Song of Songs 4:5).
2. Figuratively, the gazelle represents grace, lightness, and allure in the language of love. This poetic image recurs in the Song of Songs to describe the beauty of the bride, suggesting not only physical appearance but also elegance and tenderness. It is a language of admiration and affection, where the beloved young woman is compared to the most graceful creatures of creation.
H6646.origine: The Hebrew word צְבִיָּה (tseviyyah) is a feminine form or variant of צְבִי (tsevi), which designates the gazelle. The root expresses the idea of a shining or radiant beauty, linked to the splendor and brilliance of the animal. This word belongs to the vocabulary of nature in the Middle East, where the gazelle was a known and admired animal. The given form (tseviyyah) could also refer to the female of the gazelle.
H6646.emploi: The word gazelle (צְבִיָּה) appears twice in the Bible, only in the Song of Songs, the love song of the biblical collection. In both passages (Song of Songs 4:5 and 7:4), it serves to describe the beauty of the bride. Each time, the breasts of the beloved woman are compared to the fawns or twins of a gazelle, creating a poetic image of grace, sweetness, and harmony. This comparison assumes that the reader is familiar with the natural grace and elegance of this animal to understand the praise directed at the beloved.
H6646.portee: This image reminds us that in the Bible, human beauty is not vulgar or superficial, but can be celebrated with delicacy and poetry. The gazelle, a symbol of natural grace, invites us to recognize divine creation as beautiful and worthy of admiration. For a believer, seeing the beauty of the bride compared to creation affirms that beauty is a gift from God to be celebrated, especially within the context of marital love.

sens: make wet, soak with moisture
be soaked, be saturated with water
undergo the action of moisture, be exposed to dew
H6647.detail:
1. To soak means to cause a liquid, particularly water, to penetrate something or to be applied to something: it is to make something completely wet or saturated. In Nebuchadnezzar's dream, the tree must remain "soaked with the dew of heaven" (Daniel 4:15): the dew comes down from heaven and penetrates the trunk, soaking it continuously.
2. The word also designates the state of something that is saturated with water, which undergoes the constant action of external moisture. When it is said that Nebuchadnezzar's body "was soaked with the dew of heaven" (Daniel 4:33), it evokes a man completely exposed to the elements, night after night covered with droplets, the moisture penetrating his clothes and skin.
H6647.origine: The Hebrew verb צְבַע comes from a root that expresses the idea of deep penetration by a liquid. The word evokes the image of a liquid substance that passes through and saturates a solid — not just wetting it on the surface, but saturating it. This root is related to the concept of lasting contact between water and what it penetrates.
H6647.emploi: This verb appears five times in the book of Daniel, exclusively in chapters 4 and 5, all usages concerning Nebuchadnezzar. The context is always the same: during his punishment, the king is driven away from men and his body remains continually "soaked with the dew of heaven" (Daniel 4:15, 4:23, 4:25, 4:33; Daniel 5:21). This repetition emphasizes the prolonged and inevitable exposure of the king to the elements — the dew that penetrates him each night, reminding him of his humiliation and helplessness. The verb accentuates not a one-time act, but a state of persistent saturation.
H6647.portee: This word reminds us that Nebuchadnezzar's humiliation and abasement were not momentary, but lasting. The dew, gentle in appearance, becomes a symbol of God's patient and inevitable action on one who forgets his authority. For the Christian reader, to soak also evokes how the Word of God permeates and penetrates the heart of one who submits to it — not as violence, but as the gradual absorption of a truth that permeates the entire being.

sens: dyed fabric or colored cloth
precious and ornate garment, spoils of war
H6648.detail:
1. The word refers to the fabric itself after it has been dyed in a dye. It is the colored cloth, the result of the dyer's work. In ancient societies, dyed garments were precious and rare, as dyeing was costly and difficult to produce.
2. By extension, it refers to the garment made from this dyed fabric — a rich, ornate, and prestigious piece of clothing. In Judges 5:30, Sisera, the general of the enemy army, covets spoils consisting of "colored garments, embroidered": these are luxury garments, fruits of victory, symbolizing the wealth and social status of the warrior who possesses them.
H6648.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to dip" or "to plunge" — the image of the fabric dipped in the dye bath. It is a name that designates both the action (dyeing) and its result (the colored fabric). The word emphasizes the craftsmanship and technique required to produce these precious fabrics.
H6648.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 5:30, the Song of Deborah. In this warrior context, it refers to the spoils that victorious warriors bring back — dyed and embroidered garments, signs of wealth and prestige. The usage here highlights the contrast between the confidence of the defeated enemies (who expected to bring back luxury garments) and their unexpected defeat.
H6648.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, material possessions — even the most beautiful and precious — can be lost quickly in the reversal of circumstances. The mention of the "colored garments" coveted by Sisera serves to illustrate the vanity of the proud warrior's confidence, defeated by the hand of God through a woman, Jael.

sens: Father of Anah and grandfather of Aholibamah, wife of Esau
Man from the time of the Patriarchs, related to the Horites
H6649G.detail:
1. Zibeon is a character from the clan of the Horites, mentioned as the father of Anah in the genealogy of Esau. His daughter Anah has a daughter, Aholibamah, who becomes one of Esau's wives and the mother of several of his sons (Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah). He embodies the complex genealogical ties between the peoples of Canaan and the descendants of Isaac.
2. Zibeon belongs to the generation of the Horites, a people established in the region, and represents the marital alliances between the Hebrews and the local populations during the time of the Patriarchs.
H6649G.origine: The name Zibeon means "of varied color" or "spotted" (from the root צבע, which evokes distinctive coloring). This name likely reflects a remarkable physical characteristic, as was common in Hebrew names. The name appears in the genealogies of Esau, recalling the indigenous ancestors with whom Isaac's family united through marriage.
H6649G.emploi: Zibeon appears twice in the Bible, both in Genesis 36, in the list of descendants and alliances of Esau. In Genesis 36:2, he is designated as the father of Anah and indirectly as the father-in-law of Esau (through his granddaughter Aholibamah). In Genesis 36:14, he is mentioned again as the grandfather of Aholibamah, one of Esau's three main wives. These two mentions firmly establish his role in the Horite genealogy and his connection to the Esauite branch.

sens: A Horite chief
Son of the Horite Seir
Father of Aiah and Anah
H6649H.detail: Zibeon is a character from the time of the Patriarchs, one of the sons of Seir the Horite, an ancient people of Edom (Genesis 36:20). He appears in the genealogies of Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1 as one of the Horite chiefs who lived in the region (Genesis 36:29). He had two sons: Aiah and Anah (Genesis 36:24). Anah, his son, was the father of Aholibamah, who became one of Esau's wives, thus linking the Horites to the lineage of Abraham through marriage.
H6649H.origine: The name Zibeon means "colored" or "variegated". It designates a character from the patriarchal time, ancestor of the Horite clans. Although little known to the modern reader, Zibeon figures among the genealogies of the Bible to show the deep-rootedness of the alliances and family ties that structured the ancient world of Canaan and Edom.
H6649H.emploi: Zibeon appears five times in the Bible, always in genealogical lists. He is first named in Genesis 36:20 among the sons of Seir the Horite. Genesis 36:24 presents him as the father of Aiah and Anah, the latter having discovered hot springs while tending the donkeys. In Genesis 36:29, he is listed among the Horite chiefs. Finally, 1 Chronicles 1:38 and 1:40 repeat this genealogical information to establish the historical continuity of the peoples of Canaan.

sens: City of the tribe of Benjamin, between Jericho and Jerusalem
H6650G.detail: Tseboïm is a city inhabited after the exile, located in the territory of Benjamin. It is among the localities repopulated after the Babylonian captivity, which shows the gradual restoration of the kingdom of Judah.
H6650G.origine: The name means "the spotted ones" or "the variegated ones", likely evoking animals or terrains with a variegated pattern. It is a typical place name from the territory of Benjamin, in the region of the hills rising toward Jerusalem.
H6650G.emploi: Tseboïm appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:34, in the list of cities and villages that the people of Judah and Benjamin reclaimed after the return from exile. This mention fits into the context of the restoration of the people of Israel and their territory. It is located between Hadid and Neballat.

sens: Valley of Judah between Jericho and Jerusalem
H6650H.detail: Tseboïm is a valley in the territory of Benjamin, in ancient Judah, located between Jericho to the east and Jerusalem to the west. It formed a natural border zone, recognized as an important geographical landmark during military movements (1 Samuel 13:18).
H6650H.origine: The name means "spotted" or "mottled" in Hebrew, likely alluding to the appearance of the terrain or vegetation. It designates both a specific valley and the surrounding region in the land of Benjamin.
H6650H.emploi: Tseboïm appears only once in the Bible, in the account of Jonathan's raid against the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:18). The text mentions the valley of Tseboïm as one of the three routes by which the Philistines invaded the territory of Israel, demonstrating its strategic importance as a passage between inhabited areas and the Judean desert.

sens: To gather and heap things in quantity
To accumulate for oneself repeatedly
To pile up or stack together
H6651.detail:
1. To gather and heap things in quantity: this is the concrete action of stacking, putting together to form a heap. Joseph "gathered grain like the sand of the sea" (Genesis 41:49), meaning he accumulated it in large quantities. This also happened with the frogs in Egypt: "They were piled up in heaps" (Exodus 8:10).
2. To accumulate for oneself repeatedly: this is the act of doing it over and over again, to increase one's possessions. A man "gathers" money and piles up clothes as if he fears lacking (Job 27:16), but also, in general, "a man gathers, and he does not know who will collect it" (Psalms 39:7) — he accumulates without knowing who will benefit from it after him.
3. To pile up or stack together: the word emphasizes the formation of heaps or stacks. The enemy "piles up earth" to build ramparts (Habakkuk 1:10), accumulating earth to take the fortresses.
H6651.origine: The Hebrew verb צָבַר (tsavar) comes from a root that evokes the action of putting in heaps, of stacking. The word belongs to the family of concrete work verbs: it is a repeated hand gesture that creates a heap. The root refers to the physical image of a heap or mound.
H6651.emploi: The verb appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in contexts of material accumulation or work. In the story of Joseph, it describes the gathering of grain as provision (Genesis 41:35, 41:49). In Egypt, the frogs and plagues are "piled up" (Exodus 8:10). In the Wisdom literature, especially Job and the Psalms, "to gather" takes on a critical tone: man accumulates wealth for himself, but without knowing who will enjoy it (Psalms 39:7; Job 27:16). It is a vain gesture when it is motivated only by selfishness. Habakkuk uses it for the military action of fortification.
H6651.portee: This word poses an existential question to the Christian reader: why accumulate if we do not know who will inherit it? It invites reflection on the meaning of work and wealth. Accumulation is not bad in itself — Joseph does it to save a people — but it becomes vain when it serves only pride or fear. It is a call to work with wisdom and generosity.

sens: accumulation of objects piled on top of each other
group of things arranged together without particular order
H6652.detail:
1. The word designates an accumulation of objects piled on top of each other — what one sees when stacking things without concern for arrangement. In 2 Kings 10:8, King Jehu orders that the heads of the king's sons be put in a "heap" at the entrance of the gate: a raw and dark image of piled corpses, which testifies to the cruelty of the moment.
2. More broadly, a heap is a group of things gathered, a mound — the idea of a mass without particular order, where the elements lose their individuality in collective accumulation.
H6652.origine: The Hebrew word צִבּוּר (tsibour) comes from a root that evokes the idea of gathering or accumulating. It forms a family with other words describing gatherings, groups, or accumulations. The basic image is that of things piled up, heaped without order, different from an organized or enumerated collection.
H6652.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Kings 10:8. Jehu, king of Israel, orders the messengers to bring the heads of the murdered king's sons and to place them in two "heaps" at the entrance of the gate of Jezreel. This brutal and military context — the display of corpses as an act of domination and mockery — is the only biblical use of the word. It suggests a visible, ostentatious accumulation, intended to intimidate or humiliate.
H6652.portee: This word reminds us how Scripture bluntly names acts of violence and contempt towards the dead. Jehu, although anointed by God to end the idolatry of the house of Ahab, crosses the limits of honor here: the placing of heads in a "heap" evokes not the justice of God, but human barbarity. The attentive reader finds a lesson: religious zeal does not justify everything, and excessive cruelty tarnishes even acts begun for a just cause.

sens: A bundle or a package of stalks of grain tied together
H6653.detail: 1. A sheaf is an assembly of stalks of grain (wheat, barley, etc.) gathered and tied together for transport or storage. It is the result of the harvest work: one cuts the ears, gathers them, and ties them. In Ruth 2:16, the harvesters are asked to deliberately drop some complete sheaves so that Ruth can glean them — that is, pick them up — and thus provide for her needs.
H6653.origine: The Hebrew word צְבָתִים comes from a root that expresses the idea of binding, gathering, or tying together. A sheaf is precisely grain tied into a tight bundle. This notion of grouping and binding is at the heart of the word: several scattered stalks become a solid and transportable unit.
H6653.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ruth 2:16. It is used in the context of the harvest and the law of Israel that required leaving something for the poor and the foreigners (Ruth is a foreigner and a widow without resources). The harvesters are invited to voluntarily remove entire sheaves from the normal work of the harvest and leave them behind for Ruth to glean. It is an act of organized generosity, made possible by the abundance of the harvest.
H6653.portee: The sheaf reminds the reader that generosity towards the poor is not an isolated act, but a practice integrated into ordinary life. Dropping entire sheaves is more than simple gleaning: it is active hospitality. This word illustrates how the law of Moses protected the most vulnerable by inviting the wealthy to share the fruit of their labor.

sens: The lateral part of something, an object, or a structure
The lateral part of the body, the flank or arm
Either of the two opposite directions in a space
Near something or someone, beside
The position or orientation of a person facing a situation
H6654.detail:
1. Side refers to the lateral part of an object or structure: the ark has a side through which one enters (Genesis 6:16), the lampstand of the sanctuary has branches that extend from its sides (Exodus 37:18). It is one of the lateral faces, as opposed to the front, back, top, or bottom.
2. For the body, side means the flank or arm: Isaiah speaks of children carried on the arms ("sides") of their mother (Isaiah 66:12), the image evokes maternal protection and affection.
3. Side also expresses either of the two opposite directions in the same space: Saul walks on one side of the mountain while David flees on the other side (1 Samuel 23:26), each occupying their slope.
4. Beside or nearby: Ruth sat beside the harvesters at the meal (Ruth 2:14), which simply means near them, in their vicinity.
5. Side can also designate a position or orientation in a given situation: to occupy a side means to take a defined place or position.
H6654.origine: The word צַד (tsad) comes from a root that literally evokes what is extended, spread out on the sides. It is a simple and ancient word, common in biblical Hebrew. Aramaic uses the same word צַד with the same meaning. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it is often rendered by words meaning "side" or "flank," which shows the stability of this notion across Semitic languages.
H6654.emploi: The word צַד appears 27 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in construction narratives (the ark, the tabernacle), historical accounts, and poetry. In the descriptions of the tabernacle and its furnishings (Exodus 25, 37), it precisely designates the sides of sacred objects. In battle or pursuit narratives (1 Samuel 23:26), it situates the combatants in space. In more poetic descriptions, it takes on a more affectionate tone: being carried on the sides/arms of a mother (Isaiah 66:12) evokes tenderness. The word is also used to indicate the proximity of a person or a city (Ruth 2:14, Joshua 3:16).
H6654.portee: Knowing this word helps the reader to concretely visualize the spaces and objects described in the Bible: how the ark was constructed, how the tabernacle was organized. More broadly, the passages where one is seated or carried "beside" or "on the arms" of someone show how the Bible expresses intimacy and protection through spatial proximity. It is an invitation to feel the tenderness of God who carries us like a mother carries her child on her arms.

sens: A thing related to a field of activity or competence
Word, statement
Aspect or direction
H6655.detail:
1. A matter is a thing or question that pertains to a particular field, a file that one is dealing with. Daniel 6:4 speaks of the "matters of the kingdom": the officials seek to find an accusation against Daniel regarding the administrative and governmental matters for which he is responsible.
2. The word can also mean a word or statement made about something. In Daniel 7:25, the beast "will speak words against the Most High": the word refers to the blasphemous words it will address.
3. More broadly, matter designates a side or aspect of a situation, what can be called or qualified from a certain point of view.
H6655.origine: The Hebrew word צַד (tsad) comes from a root that evokes the idea of side or direction. In biblical Hebrew, it can designate the physical side of something, but also, by extension, a domain, a question, or an aspect of a matter. The notion of "side" naturally glides into that of "aspect" or "direction" that one can take in a judgment or accusation.
H6655.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Aramaic New Testament of the book of Daniel. In Daniel 6:4, it refers to the government matters that Daniel administers: it is a concrete and administrative use. In Daniel 7:25, it takes on the coloration of words or statements that the beast "will speak": the meaning then shifts towards enunciation, the spoken word. In both cases, it concerns a matter or question on which one can act, judge, or express oneself.
H6655.portee: This word reminds us that God judges our matters — our responsibilities, our words, our management of power. For Daniel, remaining faithful in his administrative matters allows him to escape the accusations of his enemies. It invites us to conduct with integrity all that we are responsible for, knowing that nothing escapes the divine gaze.

sens: Deliberate intention, what one has decided to do
Desired goal, conscious objective
H6656.detail:
1. The word designates an intention that one has clearly decided within oneself — what one has voluntarily chosen to do. In Daniel 3:14, Nebuchadnezzar asks Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego if they are deliberately refusing, "of deliberate intention," to serve his gods: he questions their conscious and voluntary intention.
2. More broadly, it is the goal one sets for oneself, the objective one truly pursues. The word refers to a well-considered intention, not a mechanical act.
H6656.origine: The Aramaic word צְדָא (tseda) expresses the idea of a settled intention, a resolution. It comes from a Semitic root related to the idea of goal or intention. In biblical Aramaic, it is a rare term that mainly appears in passages concerning conscious decisions.
H6656.emploi: This word appears only once in biblical Aramaic, in Daniel 3:14. Nebuchadnezzar uses it to question the three young Hebrews about the voluntary nature of their refusal. It is a term that emphasizes personal responsibility and the deliberate intention behind an act.
H6656.portee: This word reminds us that God sees beyond appearances: He discerns our true intentions. In the context of the refusal of the three young men, it shows that they act knowingly, freely, which makes their faithfulness all the more honorable. It is a lesson on the importance of sincere intention in our obedience to God.

sens: To set a hidden trap for someone to kill or harm them
To watch someone in secret to do them harm
To conspire against someone with malicious intent
H6658A.detail:
1. A trap is a deadly snare set in secret: one hides to surprise someone and do them harm. In Exodus 21:13, the law distinguishes homicide by trap (criminal) from that which occurs by accident — if a man kills another without having lain in wait, God has allowed him to fall into his hand, and the murderer can take refuge.
2. It is also the act of watching someone in secret to strike them. David says to Saul in 1 Samuel 24:12: you lay traps for me to take my life, reproaching the king for pursuing him to kill him while David himself spared his life.
3. More broadly, it is any hidden and malicious intention against someone — the secret plan of one who wishes to harm.
H6658A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of hiding, concealing. It specifically designates what is secret and dangerous: one does not see the trap until it is triggered. It is a concrete word, related to traps set in hunting or warfare — a premeditated, hidden, and deadly act of violence.
H6658A.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. Both uses show a deadly danger: in Exodus 21:13, it is a legal criterion for judging a murder (if there was a trap, it is a crime; otherwise, it is an accident), and in 1 Samuel 24:12, it is an accusation of premeditated murder — David reproaches Saul for persecuting him with the intent to kill. The word always designates an immediate and serious threat.
H6658A.portee: This word reminds the reader that God distinguishes the intention of the heart: an act of accidental death is not a crime in God's eyes, but a trap — a hidden intention to kill — is. It also emphasizes the importance of human justice: it must protect those who flee from a murderer. For the believer, it is a call to vigilance against those who wish harm in secret, and a trust that God knows the intentions.

sens: To destroy and render unusable a region, a city, or a territory
To reduce to nothing, annihilate
To leave a place completely abandoned and lifeless
H6658B.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of devastating a place, completely destroying it to render it unusable. In Zephaniah 3:6, God declares: "I have destroyed the nations; their towers are fallen; I have laid waste their streets, so that no one passes through them." It is a systematic destruction that leaves nothing standing.
2. Figuratively, "to devastate" means to reduce to nothing, to completely annihilate. The context of Zephaniah shows that it is a divine act of judgment: God devastates the peoples who have turned away from Him.
3. The final result is a place completely abandoned and lifeless, where no one lives or moves anymore. The verse emphasizes that no one passes through the ravaged streets: it is total desolation.
H6658B.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of spoiling, ruining, rendering barren. The word is related to terms denoting destruction and damage. In the biblical text, it is often used to describe the work of divine judgment on rebellious nations.
H6658B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Zephaniah 3:6, where the prophet reports God's words announcing the judgment of the nations. God asserts His sovereign power by destroying those who have forgotten Him. This prophetic context of judgment defines the only known use of this term.
H6658B.portee: This verse shows that devastation is never the result of chance in the Bible: it is the sovereign act of God against the sin and idolatry of the nations. For the reader, it serves as a reminder that God does not indefinitely tolerate rebellion and that His judgment is real and inevitable for those who abandon Him.

sens: High priest during the time of King David, son of Ahitub and father of Ahimelech
Priest who served as a sacrificer in David's government
H6659G.detail:
1. Zadok is primarily the high priest who served King David. He came from the lineage of the priest Aaron, through the branch of Eleazar. He joined David after the death of Saul and remained faithful to him, especially when Absalom rebelled against his father: Zadok carried the ark of the covenant out of Jerusalem during this crisis (2 Samuel 15:24-25). Later, he anointed Solomon as king, pouring holy oil on his head as a sign of divine election (1 Kings 1:39).
2. Zadok is also simply referred to as a priest in the royal administration. Alongside other priests like Abiathar, he officiated at the temple and participated in sacred services. His name regularly appears alongside other royal officials: secretaries, generals, advisors (1 Chronicles 24:3, where David classifies him among the descendants of Eleazar in charge of the service).
H6659G.origine: The name Zadok means "just" or "the Just" in Hebrew, deriving its meaning from the word for "justice" or "righteousness." This name likely reflects the character expected of a high priest: a righteous man, in accordance with God's will. The name carried spiritual value, like many Hebrew names that expressed an ideal or a blessing.
H6659G.emploi: Zadok is mentioned about 40 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. He first appears as a priest during David's time (2 Samuel 8:17), then becomes a key figure during Solomon's succession: he is the one who anoints the young prince king in 1 Kings 1:39, while Abiathar supports his rival Adonijah. After this turning point, Zadok becomes the sole high priest, Abiathar being removed (1 Kings 2:35). The Book of Chronicles, written later, reports how David classified him among the priests of Eleazar by reorganizing them for temple service (1 Chronicles 24:3). Later, the prophet Ezekiel refers to the "sons of Zadok" as the model of faithful priests who kept God's statutes (Ezekiel 40:46, Ezekiel 44:15).
H6659G.portee: Zadok embodies faithfulness in the service of God and the king whom he has legitimately anointed. His choice during Solomon's succession shows how God supports the king according to His heart: Zadok recognizes divine election and acts accordingly, while other priests go astray. His lineage remains in later Jewish tradition a symbol of priestly authenticity and alignment with divine will.

sens: father of Jerusha, mother of King Jotham of Judah
H6659H.detail: Zadok is a name that means "the just" in Hebrew. In the provided biblical uses, it designates the father of Jerusha (or Jerusalem), wife of King Uzziah of Judah and mother of King Jotham. It appears in the royal genealogies of Judah to establish the lineage of the kings (2 Kings 15:33 and 2 Chronicles 27:1).
H6659H.origine: The name Zadok comes from the Hebrew root צדק (tsedaqah), which means "justice" or "righteousness." It is the same word that gives "tsadiq" (just), very common in biblical wisdom to designate one who lives according to God's law. The name thus carries a positive moral connotation, marking one who embodies righteousness.
H6659H.emploi: Zadok appears twice in the Bible, always in the context of the royal genealogies of Judah. He is mentioned exclusively as the father of Jerusha, the wife of King Uzziah (or Azariah) and mother of King Jotham, in the 8th century B.C. These two occurrences (2 Kings 15:33 and 2 Chronicles 27:1) are parallel and aim to establish the legitimate lineage of the kings of Judah. The name is only known to us through this genealogical link; no action or word of this Zadok is reported.

sens: High priest during the time of David and Solomon, son of Ahitub from the house of Eleazar
Levitical priest, son of Merajoth, father of Meshullam
Father of Jerusha, wife of King Uzziah and mother of King Jotham
Restorer of the wall of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
H6659I.detail:
1. Tsadok is the most famous high priest of the time of the united kingdom. Son of Ahitub, he belongs to the lineage of Eleazar, son of Aaron, and is a direct descendant of the first priests of Israel. He supports King David, particularly against the revolt of Absalom, and plays a decisive role in anointing Solomon as king (1 Chronicles 6:12 mentions his father Ahitub and his son Ahitub, placing Tsadok at the heart of a famous succession of high priests).
2. Another Tsadok bears the title of priest and is the son of Merajoth, father of the priest Meshullam. This man also belongs to the elevated priestly lineage (1 Chronicles 9:11 and Nehemiah 11:11 place him at the head of the house of God after the return from exile).
3. A Tsadok is the father of Jerusha, who became the wife of King Uzziah of Judah and the mother of King Jotham, linking him to royalty even though he is not a king himself.
4. Several other bearers of the name participate in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, showing that this name continues to be held by men of responsibility in the restored community.
H6659I.origine: The name Tsadok means "just" or "the just one," derived from the Hebrew root sādēq (צדק), which expresses justice and righteousness. This name perfectly aligns with the role of high priest, mediator between God and the people, who must embody divine justice. The family of Tsadok remains one of the most influential in the Israelite priesthood, especially after the Babylonian exile.
H6659I.emploi: Tsadok is best known as the high priest during the time of David and Solomon, who profoundly marked the religious history of Israel. The four biblical references show that his descendants held important positions in the priesthood: his son Ahitub (Ezra 7:2) and his descendants occupy the role of "prince of the house of God" (1 Chronicles 9:11, Nehemiah 11:11). After the exile to Babylon, the "house of Tsadok" becomes synonymous with legitimate and faithful priesthood. The name is also held by other less prominent figures, including those who repaired the wall under Nehemiah, demonstrating how a great ancient name extends to several descendants or namesakes of lesser importance.
H6659I.portee: Tsadok embodies the continuity of faithful priesthood in Israel. His life shows that a servant of God must remain loyal to the king anointed by the Lord, even in political crises. For the Christian reader, the lineage of Tsadok foreshadows the importance of just priestly mediation and prefigures the priesthood of Jesus Christ, who ultimately fulfills the perfect justice that no human priest could accomplish.

sens: Man of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
One whose name means "just" or "the just one"
H6659J.detail:
1. Tsadok is a man mentioned during the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He appears in Nehemiah 3:4 as one of the workers who participated in the repairs of the city walls alongside Meremoth and Meshullam.
2. His name, Tsadok, carries the meaning "the just" or "justice" — a profound significance for a man involved in the reconstruction of Jerusalem, a symbol of the restoration of God's people in righteousness and order.
H6659J.origine: The name Tsadok comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to be just," "to be righteous." It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, carrying the idea of justice and righteousness. Several Tsadoks are mentioned in the Bible — notably the high priest who supported David and anointed Solomon — but this Tsadok is the son of Baana, a minor figure during the time of Nehemiah.
H6659J.emploi: Tsadok, son of Baana, appears only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 3:4. He is one of the many craftsmen and inhabitants of Jerusalem who, under Nehemiah's leadership, accomplished the extraordinary work of rebuilding the destroyed walls of the city. His name simply appears in the list of workers, with no additional details about his role or family. He represents those ordinary men whose patient and faithful work was essential to the restoration of Jerusalem after the exile.
H6659J.portee: This brief passage reminds us that every service rendered to the Lord and His people counts, even if it is not spectacular. Tsadok, though obscure, put his hands to work to restore the holy city — a simple yet powerful lesson: ordinary faithfulness in small tasks is as precious as that of leaders.

sens: Man who repaired the wall of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
Son of Immer
H6659K.detail:
1. Tsadok is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He worked on the restoration of this fortification, fulfilling his part in this great collective work organized by Governor Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:29).
2. He is identified as the son of Immer, which anchors him in a precise genealogy. The context of Nehemiah 3 lists the various contributors to the wall project, each assigned to a particular section to work "in front of his house."
H6659K.origine: The name Tsadok means "the just" or "righteous" in Hebrew, derived from the root tsedek which denotes justice and uprightness. It is a theophoric name carrying moral and spiritual significance. Several important characters in the Old Testament bore this name, notably the high priest Tsadok during the reign of King David, but this one in Nehemiah 3:29 is a different incarnation, a simple citizen engaged in a communal task.
H6659K.emploi: Tsadok appears only once in the holy Scriptures, in Nehemiah 3:29, during the detailed account of the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem. This passage is part of a long list of those who participated in this crucial project for the restoration of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. The fact that he is named individually shows that even ordinary workers deserved recognition for their contribution to this great collective rebuilding effort.
H6659K.portee: This short verse reminds us that God sees and honors the faithful work of each person, even those who never became famous. Tsadok was neither a high priest nor a leader, but his participation in the restoration of Jerusalem places him in the holy annals. It is an encouragement for believers: humble and persevering service, accomplished in obedience to God, has lasting value in the eyes of the Lord.

sens: High priest during the time of David and Solomon, of the lineage of Aaron
H6659L.detail: Tsadok is an important figure in the history of Israel, high priest during the reign of King David. He descends from the priestly family of Aaron through Eleazar. He supports David after the death of Saul, defends him against the revolt of Absalom and Adonijah, and anoints Solomon as king. His name means "just" in Hebrew, which suits his role as guardian of worship and religious justice in Israel.
H6659L.origine: The name Tsadok literally means "just" or "righteous" in Hebrew, formed from the root צדק (tsadak), which expresses justice and uprightness. This name reflects the moral responsibility of the high priest. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament: descendants of the original high priest, other priests, and officials during the time of Nehemiah.
H6659L.emploi: Tsadok first appears as the high priest serving King David, then continues under Solomon. He comes from the house of Eleazar, a prestigious line of Aaronic priesthood. In the course of history, several other men bear the same name (repairers of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, a leader of the people, a scribe-treasurer). In Nehemiah 10:21, a Tsadok signs the people's covenant with God upon their return from exile, testifying to the continuity of this honorable name through generations.
H6659L.portee: Tsadok embodies faithfulness in the service of God and the king established by the Lord. His support of David in crises, his anointing of Solomon, and the presence of his descendants among the restorers of Jerusalem after the exile show how God preserves a faithful lineage throughout history. His name, "just," reminds us that true divine service rests on moral integrity and righteousness.

sens: Scribe and treasurer of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
Name literally meaning 'the righteous'
H6659M.detail:
1. Tsadok is a figure from the time of Nehemiah, designated as a scribe and placed in charge of overseeing the storerooms or treasures of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 13:13). He was known for his faithfulness and worked alongside the priest Shelemiah and the Levite Pedaiah to distribute portions to other Levites and priests.
