In Hebrew, the verb can take two forms: simple (the water flows by itself) or causative (one makes the water flow, one causes the flow). This root expresses the action of waters in all their power.
H6687.emploi: The verb צוּף appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, in contexts related to water and its movement. In Deuteronomy 11:4, it describes how God made the waters of the Red Sea flow over the Egyptian army — an act of destruction by the flood. In 2 Kings 6:6, it means to make float: it is a miracle of restoration where a submerged object comes back to the surface. In Lamentations 3:54, the waters flow over the one who speaks, an image of being engulfed in distress. The meaning varies between: letting flow (water that flows naturally), making float (bringing to the surface), and engulfing (submerging in the waves).
H6687.portee: This word reminds us that water, a source of life, can become an instrument of judgment or deliverance according to God's will. It illustrates divine power over creation: God can make water flow to save His people (the Red Sea) or to destroy His enemies. It also shows that the Lord can reverse the natural order of things — making iron float, which is heavy — to accomplish His wonders.

sens: Honeycomb in a hive, wax structure containing honey
Figuratively, that which is sweet and pleasant like honey
H6688.detail:
1. The honeycomb is the wax structure that bees build in their hive to store honey. It is an image of sweetness and delight: in Psalms 19:11, God's commandments are compared to the honey from the honeycomb, a symbol of what is tasty and precious.
2. By extension, 'honeycomb' also refers to that which is sweet and pleasant to the taste or to the soul. In Proverbs 16:24, 'a honeycomb' represents pleasant and beneficial words: they nourish the soul just as honey nourishes the body.
H6688.origine: The Hebrew word צוּף (tsuph) designates the part of honey that can be consumed directly, the wax honeycomb filled with honey. Its etymology refers to the idea of 'flowing' or 'pouring out,' as honey flows from the honeycomb. In Hebrew, it is a classic poetic figure to express what is sweet, tasty, and precious.
H6688.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 19:11, it expresses the sweetness of divine precepts, compared to pure honey flowing from the honeycomb: this indicates how desirable and delightful God's Word is for those who enjoy it. In Proverbs 16:24, it illustrates the beneficial effect of sweet and kind words, which soothe the soul and restore the body. In both cases, the image of the honeycomb conveys a reality that is both sensory (the sweet taste) and spiritual (the deep satisfaction).
H6688.portee: This word reminds us that God's Word and just words are not burdens, but sources of joy and life. Meditating on the Torah, listening to the commandments, practicing sweetness in our words: these are not bitter obligations, but delights that truly nourish our soul and body. It is an invitation to taste the goodness of God.

sens: Levitical ancestor of the prophet Samuel
Mountainous region of Ephraim where Saul met Samuel
H6689G.detail: 1. Tsuph is a man of the tribe of Levi, ancestor of the prophet Samuel. He appears in the genealogy of Elkanah, the father of Samuel: Tsuph is the grandfather of Tohu, from whom Elkanah descends (1 Samuel 1:1). He is also called Tsoplaï in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 6:26), where the lineage of the Kohathite Levites clearly names him as the ancestor of Elkanah and, through him, of the prophet Samuel. 2. Tsuph also designates a mountainous region in the territory of Ephraim, located northwest of Jerusalem. It is there that Saul met the prophet Samuel when he was searching for his donkeys (1 Samuel 9). This region bears the name of the Levitical ancestor, suggesting that the descendants of Tsuph owned land there or exercised their ministry.
H6689G.origine: The name Tsuph means 'honeycomb' or 'honey cake,' formed from the root צוף (tsuph) which refers to the idea of sweetness and abundance. This same name appears in the variant Tsoplaï (1 Chronicles 6:26), which is an augmented form of the same element. The meaning 'honey' or 'honeycomb' has remained transparent in tradition, recalling both divine abundance and the genealogy of Israel's greatest prophet before David.
H6689G.emploi: Tsuph is mentioned three times in the Bible, always in a genealogical or geographical context. In 1 Samuel 1:1, he appears in the direct genealogy of Elkanah, father of Samuel, establishing his place in the Kohathite Levitical lineage. In 1 Chronicles 6:26 and 6:35, the Chronicler resumes this genealogy with more details, confirming that Tsuph was a prestigious ancestor of the prophet and high priest Samuel. The name is also used to designate the region of Ramathaim-Zophim (literally 'the two heights of Tsuph'), where the family of Elkanah lived, showing that this Levitical clan had a territory of influence in the mountains of Ephraim.

sens: mountainous region of the territory of Ephraim, northwest of Jerusalem
H6689H.detail: Tsuph is a region of Palestine mentioned only once in the Bible. Its name means "ray of honey" or "honeycomb," perhaps evoking a fertile and rich land. It is in this region that Saul, the future king of Israel, and his servant find themselves in search of his father's lost donkeys (1 Samuel 9:5); it is also where the prophet Samuel lived.
H6689H.origine: The name Tsuph comes from a root that evokes honey and sweetness, suggesting a fertile and generous land. The same term or a similar form can refer to a ray of honey, an image that conveys the idea of abundance and natural wealth.
H6689H.emploi: Tsuph appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 9:5. It is mentioned as a district or region that Saul accidentally passes through while searching for his father's donkeys. This geographical detail situates the action of the narrative and shows how Saul, unknowingly, draws closer to his decisive encounter with the prophet Samuel, who lived in this region.

sens: Man from the tribe of Asher during the divided monarchy
H6690.detail: Tsophach is an Assyrian (a man from the tribe of Asher), living during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Helem (or Hotham) and the father of at least eleven children, including Suach, Harnépher, and Schual. He is mentioned in the genealogies of Asher in 1 Chronicles 7:35-36, where his descendants are listed.
H6690.origine: The name Tsophach literally means "a pitcher" or "a vessel." It is a typical Hebrew name that can evoke a concrete image, similar to many ancient biblical names.
H6690.emploi: Tsophach appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 7:35-36, in the genealogical record of the tribe of Asher. He is a minor figure in biblical history, known primarily through the list of his descendants. No event or action is associated with him in the biblical text.

sens: One of the three friends who came to comfort Job in his suffering
A man from Naamah who intervenes in the dialogue of the book of Job
H6691.detail:
1. Tsophar is one of Job's three friends, along with Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite. When Job loses his possessions, his children, and his health, these three men learn of his misfortunes and conspire to come and mourn with him and comfort him (Job 2:11). He is initially a character of compassion, responding to the call of friendly duty.
2. Tsophar from Naamah speaks during the great dialogue of the book. He intervenes at least twice to respond to Job, notably to defend the idea that God punishes the wicked (Job 11:1 and Job 20:1). At the end of the book, he obeys the command of the Lord (Job 42:9), showing his ability to submit to divine will despite his errors in judgment.
H6691.origine: The name Tsophar means "sparrow" or "small bird" in Hebrew, an image of smallness or fragility. This character belongs to the ancient tradition of the Near East during the time of the Patriarchs, although the book of Job is a complex sapiential composition. The three friends symbolize human wisdom confronted with the mystery of innocent suffering.
H6691.emploi: Tsophar appears four times in the book of Job. He is first presented alongside the other two friends as a comforter (Job 2:11), then he speaks twice in the dialogue to express his thoughts on divine justice and the fate of the wicked (Job 11 and Job 20). Finally, he is among those who, after the final word of the Lord, carry out His commands and see the Lord grant His grace to Job (Job 42:9). His role illustrates how friendship and human wisdom can be mistaken, but how submission to God corrects the path.
H6691.portee: Tsophar represents the danger of hasty religious certainty: one can come to comfort a friend with the best intentions, but defend a rigid theology that judges rather than truly listens to suffering. His example invites the believer to remain humble in the face of life's mysteries and to recognize the limits of their understanding, while remaining open to the correction that God brings.

sens: To produce flowers, to be covered with flowers
To grow, to blossom, to prosper
To shine, to radiate, to gleam
H6692A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is botanical: a plant blooms when it produces its flowers. This is the image of Aaron's rod in Numbers 17:8, which not only blooms but also bears fruit (almonds), a miraculous sign of its priestly legitimacy.
2. Figuratively, to bloom means to prosper, to experience growth and abundance. Men "bloom" in cities (Psalms 72:16), just as green grass thrives in the sun. It is the state of a life that flourishes, that asserts itself.
3. To bloom can also express brilliance and shine. In Psalms 132:18, the crown of the king "shines" upon him, resplendent with glory. It is less about vegetation and more about light and magnificence that burst forth.
H6692A.origine: The Hebrew verb צוּץ (tsuts) evokes the bursting forth of life: the plant that unfolds into flowers, showing its vital energy. It is related to images of germ, shoot, and visible manifestation. The word expresses what illuminates, what emerges before the eyes in a brilliant and lively manner.
H6692A.emploi: This verb appears about 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Psalms and prophetic books. It describes either the ephemeral cycle of nature (the grass that blooms in the morning and withers in the evening in Psalms 90:6, the fragility of humanity in Psalms 103:15), or the flourishing of the wicked who temporarily prosper before ruin (Psalms 92:8). It also carries a sense of honor and royal splendor (Psalms 132:18). The miracle of Aaron's rod (Numbers 17:8) is the pinnacle of this: to bloom becomes proof of divine power and legitimacy.
H6692A.portee: This word reminds the believer of the beauty and ephemerality of earthly life. To bloom is to live intensely but briefly. It invites one not to cling to the fleeting prosperity of the wicked, but to seek the eternal radiance that comes from God. For those who follow the Lord, it promises true flourishing, rooted in divine wisdom rather than in momentary success.

sens: To observe attentively, to take a glance
To catch a glimpse, to spy through an opening
To let the gaze shine, to make the eyes sparkle
H6692B.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of looking with attention and liveliness. It is to observe something or someone by fixing one's eyes upon them. In Song of Solomon 2:9, the lover "looks through the window," meaning he observes, he takes an attentive glance.
2. The word often suggests a furtive, discreet look, peering through an opening. It evokes the idea of looking without being entirely visible, to spy or catch a glimpse. This sense dominates in Song of Solomon 2:9: the lover "looks through the lattice," catching sight of his beloved through a grille.
3. By extension, the verb can also express the brilliance of the gaze, the liveliness of eyes that shine or sparkle, as if the gaze itself emitted light. It is an image of love and tenderness that radiates through the eyes.
H6692B.origine: The verb צוּץ (tsuts) comes from a root that evokes the idea of bursting forth or shining. The form used here (Hiphil) gives a causative or intensive sense: not only to look, but to make the gaze shine or render it visible. The word belongs to the family of verbs that describe the action of seeing with liveliness and intensity.
H6692B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 2:9. In this passage from the most lyrical of biblical books, it describes the lover looking at his beloved, first through the window, then through the lattice. The context is one of romantic encounter where the gaze is filled with tenderness and desire. The verb emphasizes the liveliness and intensity of the loving gaze, its ardent and attentive character.
H6692B.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, the gaze is never neutral: it expresses love, desire, the attention we give to someone. For the Christian reader, it invites reflection on the power of the loving gaze and how our attention to others reveals our heart. It is also an image of the tenderness and sweetness that characterize true love.

sens: To subject someone to strong pressure, to a constraint that crushes
To torment, to harass someone persistently to make them yield
To besiege a city, to reduce it to extreme distress through deprivation
To press inwardly, to urge with urgency
H6693.detail:
1. The primary meaning describes a force that crushes, that reduces to helplessness: it is the action of an enemy who "reduces" a people to famine by threatening their walls (Deuteronomy 28:53). The pressure is total, external, and violent.
2. The verb is also used for repeated moral oppression: Samson is "tormented" day after day by Delilah, who relentlessly harasses him to extract his secret (Judges 16:16). It is not a brutal blow, but an insistence that exhausts.
3. To besiege means to encircle a city in a military vise until it is drained of resources: references in Isaiah and Jeremiah speak of cities that are pressed, surrounded, and famished.
4. The word also describes an almost irresistible inner pressure: Job says that the spirit "presses" within him, like a force that rises and demands to be expressed (Job 32:18).
H6693.origine: The root צוּק (tsuq) evokes the fundamental idea of tightening, reducing space. It expresses everything that constricts, compresses, or encircles. The form used here (Hiphil) intensifies the meaning: it does not merely say "to be tight" (simple form), but "to make tight," "to impose pressure." This root does not have a single simple Greek equivalent, but it is close to the idea of "straitness" — the state of being cramped, without escape.
H6693.emploi: The verb appears about 10 times in the Bible, mainly in Deuteronomy and the prophets. In the threats of Deuteronomy 28, it paints the terrible picture of a siege: an enemy who presses the people until they resort to cannibalism, so extreme is the famine. In Judges, it describes personal harassment: Delilah "torments" Samson day after day to learn the secret of his strength. In poetry, in Job and Isaiah, the verb extends to moral and spiritual pressure: a feeling that grips you from within. Each time, it is a constraint with no way out, whether military, personal, or internal.
H6693.portee: This word reminds us that oppression — whether it comes from outside or creeps from within — is a grave sin that destroys humanity. It also highlights the real suffering of victims of siege and famine: the Bible does not hide the horror. For the Christian, it is a call to refuse to press others and to seek protection in God in the face of those who attempt to crush us.

sens: To change a solid material to a liquid state through heat
To pour, to let a liquid flow
To spread, to disperse something
To seek ardently, turning towards someone
H6694.detail:
1. The verb first denotes the physical action of melting a mineral or stone under heat to extract metal: in Job 28:2, it speaks of the stone that "melts" to produce bronze, meaning it is heated until it releases the metal it contains.
2. It also means to pour or let a liquid flow. In Job 29:6, the rock "spreads" streams of oil: the image is of the rock letting oil flow like a spring.
3. By extension, the verb can express the idea of spreading or dispersing. The meaning of pouring expands beyond liquids to describe a flow or profusion.
4. In Isaiah 26:16, the verb takes on a figurative nuance: "to seek" someone means to turn towards them with ardor and insistence, as one seeks to reach something. The underlying idea is that of an intense search, an aspiration that "pours" or spills out towards God in distress.
H6694.origine: The Hebrew verb צוּק (tsuq) comes from a root that evokes the idea of pouring, flowing, or melting. Its primary image is that of liquid flowing or material changing state. The verb thus expresses a movement of passage from one state to another, notably the transformation of solid to liquid or the pouring of a liquid. This root is linked to the idea of flow and continuous movement.
H6694.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in poetic or sapiential contexts (Job and Isaiah). In Job 28:2, it describes the technical process of melting ores. In Job 29:6, it paints a poetic image of abundance. In Isaiah 26:16, it shifts to a figurative or abstract sense: seeking God means turning to Him with ardor. These three usages show how the verb evolves from the concrete (melting a stone, pouring a substance) to the figurative (seeking with intensity, giving oneself entirely to a quest).
H6694.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on transformation and ardor. Melting an ore illustrates the process by which raw material becomes precious; similarly, trials melt the human heart so that it emerges pure. In Isaiah 26:16, the idea of seeking God in distress reminds us that a true search for God is an act of totality, of spiritual intensity that cannot be superficial.

sens: Time of distress, pressing difficulty
Narrow situation that confines and suffocates
H6695A.detail: 1. The word describes a situation of oppression or constraint that weighs heavily: it is a difficult, tight time, where freedom is reduced. In Daniel 9:25, the "troublesome times" during which Jerusalem will be rebuilt evoke a period of trials, tension, perhaps external threats or hostile conditions that will accompany the restoration. 2. The basic image is that of a narrow space that constricts: the word suggests a kind of vise, an inevitable pressure. This is why it applies well to moments of distress or moral anguish, where one feels trapped by circumstances.
H6695A.origine: The Hebrew word צוֹק (tsoq) comes from a root that means "to tighten" or "to press." It shares a kinship with words describing physical constraint and narrowness. The fundamental image is that of a throat or a narrow passage — a place where one is confined. This image naturally extends to the idea of being trapped or oppressed, hence its application to moral distress or difficult circumstances.
H6695A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 9:25, in the context of the famous prophecy of the seventy weeks. The prophet Daniel receives a revelation about the stages of the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the exile. The expression "in troublesome times" qualifies the period of the sixty-two weeks: despite the promise of restoration, this rebuilding will not occur in peace, but under oppression or in adverse conditions. This is an important nuance of the prophecy — deliverance is not simple or radiant, but mixed with difficulties.
H6695A.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's promises do not always eliminate trials or hostile circumstances. The rebuilding of Jerusalem did indeed take place, but in a context of constraint: it is an invitation to persevere in trust even when times are "troublesome." For the Christian, this sheds light on the idea that the fulfillment of God's purposes can coexist with tribulation, and that faith does not guarantee the absence of difficulties, but rather the certainty that God will accomplish His plan despite everything.

sens: State of physical or moral oppression that suffocates
Situation of distress and imminent danger
Feeling of deep anxiety in the face of inevitable evils
H6695B.detail:
1. Anguish is primarily a physical sensation of oppression, as if one is crushed or suffocated by an external force — the translation of the original word evokes the idea of "pressure." It can emanate from a storm or a natural disaster that overwhelms someone (Proverbs 1:27).
2. Anguish refers to a situation of total distress, the moment when misfortune falls upon one who cannot escape. It accumulates: the prophet Isaiah speaks of "dark anguishes" that thicken in the darkness, like an oppressive obscurity (Isaiah 8:22).
3. It also expresses the anxiety that invades a people in peril, confronted with a dangerous path: anguish accompanies one who traverses an inhospitable land filled with wild beasts, without resources or hope (Isaiah 30:6).
H6695B.origine: The Hebrew word צוּקָה (tsuqah) comes from a root meaning "to press," "to squeeze," "to crush." This image of compression or a vise corresponds exactly to what one feels in anguish: an oppression that tightens the throat and heart. The same root produces other Hebrew words expressing distress and constriction.
H6695B.emploi: This word appears three times in the prophetic and wisdom books of the Old Testament. In Proverbs, anguish is one of the consequences that falls upon one who rejects wisdom. In Isaiah, it becomes an image of God's judgment: it descends upon a people who have turned away from Him, also operating in a landscape of desolation (a difficult pilgrimage path). Anguish always appears linked to an impossible situation, with no visible escape.
H6695B.portee: This word helps the reader recognize the reality of moral and spiritual distress. It shows that the absence of wisdom and unfaithfulness to God produce a concrete anguish, an oppression that can be felt. At the same time, it reveals that God knows this suffering and uses it to call man back to Him: it is a cry of alert rather than an irrevocable condemnation.

sens: Surround a fortified city to conquer it or force it to surrender
To squeeze, enclose, hold tightly in hands or in a confined space
To confine, restrict, deprive of freedom of movement
To surround, encircle in a figurative or spiritual sense
H6696A.detail:
1. To besiege a city means to surround it with an army to prevent it from communicating with the outside and to force it to surrender. The king of Assyria "besieged" Samaria for three years (2 Kings 17:5): his troops surrounded it, cutting off all supplies. This is the most frequent use of the word in the Bible, especially in war narratives.
2. To squeeze means to hold something firmly in one's hand or a container. Naaman "squeezed" two talents of silver into two bags (2 Kings 5:23): he secured them tightly. It is an image of what is kept enclosed, compressed, restrained.
3. To confine means to put someone or something in a space from which one cannot escape. The word describes the state of one who is deprived of freedom of movement, squeezed on all sides.
4. Figuratively, to completely surround in speaking of divine protection or presence: the psalmist cries, "You surround me behind and before, and lay your hand upon me" (Psalms 139:5). Here, the encirclement evokes God's attentive guard.
H6696A.origine: The Hebrew root tsur means literally "to form a circle around," hence "to enclose," "to embrace." The central image is that of an enclosure or barrier that imprisons. The word describes the action of reducing, compressing, confining by closing access. This same root appears in several Hebrew words related to closure, encirclement, and fortifications.
H6696A.emploi: The verb is used 32 times in the Bible, mainly in the historical books (Kings, Chronicles, Samuel) and prophetic books (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). Its primary and dominant meaning is "to besiege a city": it is a common military tactic under the monarchies of Israel and Judah. The texts often mention the king of Assyria or Babylon besieging a city (Samaria, Jerusalem, Rabbah). The word can also mean "to squeeze" in hands (Deuteronomy 14:25, 2 Kings 5:23), or figuratively in a spiritual sense: the benevolent encirclement of God (Psalms 139:5). In the context of war, the word carries the idea of deprivation: those besieged lack supplies and cannot escape.
H6696A.portee: This word reminds us that siege is a formidable reality of ancient life: isolation, deprivation, possible death. For the believer, it can also speak of how God "surrounds" him — not to crush him, but to protect him and never let him go. Understanding what it meant to be besieged helps to read prophetic threats (Jeremiah on besieged Jerusalem) and the faith that endures despite encirclement.

sens: To show hostility towards someone, seek to harm them
To be the enemy, the adversary of someone
To take up arms against, engage in combat
H6696B.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes an attitude of hostility: to show that one is the enemy of someone, to harm them or seek to do so. This is why Exodus 23:22 speaks of the Lord who will be "the adversary of your adversaries" — He will position Himself as an enemy against those who attack you.
2. From this meaning derives that of "to fight" or "to engage in combat": when one shows hostility, one often moves to military action. Deuteronomy 2:9 and 2:19 prohibit Israel from engaging in combat against Moab and the Ammonites, that is, from attacking them militarily.
3. The word can also refer to the weapons themselves — the instrument of the attack. In Esther 8:11, those who "take up arms to attack them" refer to those who would rise up in arms against the Jews.
H6696B.origine: The root צור (tsur) fundamentally evokes the idea of squeezing, besieging, blocking. From this derives the meaning of "to show hostility" or "to stand as an enemy." The verb appears mainly in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in the historical and legislative books, with this constant warrior nuance.
H6696B.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible. Two occurrences are found in Deuteronomy (2:9 and 2:19), where the Lord commands Israel not to attack Moab or the Ammonites, despite possible provocations. One occurrence is in Exodus 23:22, where God promises to be the adversary of those who attack Israel. The last, in Esther 8:11, speaks of peoples who would take up arms to attack the Jews. In all cases, the word carries the connotation of active hostility and often of military action.
H6696B.portee: This verb reminds us that hostility — standing as an enemy against someone — is a reality that God's people encounter. But it also shows that God personally engages alongside His people: He will become the enemy of their enemies. This is a source of assurance for the believer who trusts in God: he is never alone in the face of those who fight against him.

sens: give form to a material by working it
create by assembling elements
produce a work of art or an object
H6696C.detail:
1. The word describes the action of working a raw material — stone, metal, wood — to give it a precise and useful shape. It is the gesture of the sculptor or the blacksmith who shapes his work. In 1 Kings 7:15, King Solomon "made" the two large bronze pillars of the Temple by casting and working them to obtain imposing and regular structures.
2. More broadly, shaping means creating or producing an object by assembling or transforming materials. The verb does not only mean "to carve" but "to bring forth," "to form a creation." This is why it applies to both metal casting and sculpture.
3. The underlying image is that of a human intention realized in the material: the creator has a vision and makes it visible. This implies skill, planning, and the will to achieve a precise result.
H6696C.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the action of giving form, of shaping. The same family includes the noun צוּר (tsur), which can mean "rock" or "stone" — the quintessential raw material that the sculptor must shape. This etymological link shows that the verb starts from the image of stone and the patient work of the sculptor.
H6696C.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible according to the provided references: in Exodus 32:4, to describe the making of the golden calf (Aaron "made" the calf by casting it), and in 1 Kings 7:15, where Solomon's workers "made" the bronze pillars of the Temple. In both cases, it involves the work of molten metal cast into a form. The word emphasizes the technical mastery and creative intention of the artisan.
H6696C.portee: For the reader, this verb reminds us that every valuable object requires work and skill. In a biblical context, it also questions the difference between the object created by man (even beautiful and impressive) and what truly deserves to be worshiped: the golden calf is "shaped" by human hands, while God alone creates by speaking. It is an invitation not to confuse human work with the divine.

sens: natural rock formation, cliff or crag
place of refuge or protection
symbol of solidity and stability
H6697G.detail:
1. A rock is a natural stone formation, often a cliff or crag. In the text, Saul searches for David on the "rocks of the wild goats," meaning in a mountainous and rocky area where wild animals take refuge.
2. The rock represents a place of refuge and safety: it is a difficult-to-access spot where one can hide and protect oneself. David finds a natural hiding place there against Saul who is pursuing him.
3. In the Bible, the rock symbolizes solidity, firmness, and trust: it represents something unchanging and reliable, on which one can depend.
H6697G.origine: The word rock comes from a root that evokes the idea of hardness and solidity. In Hebrew, צוּר (tsur) refers to the very nature of stone: something hard, resistant, that cannot be altered. The same root is found in other Hebrew words that describe strength and protection.
H6697G.emploi: The word rock appears once in this passage from 1 Samuel. David flees from Saul and hides in the caves of the rocks near Ein-Gedi, a desert and rugged region where the cliffs provide natural shelters. This context shows that the rock is primarily a physical, concrete place that protects the fugitive. It is in these crevices and rocky cavities that David can escape from his pursuers.
H6697G.portee: For the reader, this passage reminds us that places of protection, even natural ones, can be signs of God's providence. Saul will not find David on the rocks, illustrating how God keeps His servants safe in dangerous situations. The rock thus becomes a symbol of security for those who place their trust in God.

sens: mass of natural stone, hardened and compact, forming a mountain, cliff, or isolated block
rocky wall, crag, or cavity carved in stone
smooth or slightly flat surface of natural stone
place of refuge or protection in the rocks
God Himself, compared to a stable and unshakeable rock
solid foundation on which one relies with confidence
H6697H.detail:
1. The rock is the mass of raw stone that God created: it is the mountain, the cliff, or the large stone encountered in nature. At Horeb, Moses struck the rock to bring forth water (Exodus 17:6), or God asked Joshua for stone knives to circumcise the children of Israel (Joshua 5:2).
2. The rock refers to rocky walls: the "clefts of the rocks" or the "hollows of the stones" where men seek to hide (Isaiah 2:21).
3. The rock can be smooth, with a flat surface from which water and honey flow (Psalms 81:17: "I would satisfy him with honey from the rock").
4. The rock becomes a place of refuge and physical safety: when David flees from his enemies, he asks God to be his rock and fortress (Psalms 28:1; 2 Samuel 22:3).
5. God Himself is called "rock" to express His unshakeable stability and protective strength: "My rock! Do not be deaf to my voice" (Psalms 28:1) or "The Lord is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer" (2 Samuel 22:2-3).
6. The rock figures the solid foundation of trust in God: the man who relies on God stands on a rock, something permanent and reliable (Isaiah 26:4: "Trust in the Lord forever, For the Lord is the rock of ages").
H6697H.origine: The Hebrew word צוּר (tsur) designates the raw and compact stone, as it emerges from the ground. Its primary image is that of an unassailable and durable material. In biblical Hebrew, this term contrasts with loose earth or sand: it is what remains, what endures. The related Aramaic tur (טוּר) means "mountain." In the Hebrew Bible, the rock gradually becomes a powerful metaphor: from a physical object, it becomes the symbol of God Himself, stable, eternal, and trustworthy.
H6697H.emploi: The word "rock" appears 73 times in the Hebrew text of the Bible. It is mostly found in the Psalms (which celebrate God as rock), in Deuteronomy, and in the historical books (which mention rocks as places of refuge or miracle). Literally, the rock is primarily a geographical reality: the mountain, the cliff, or the stone used (Joshua 5:2; Isaiah 2:21). However, the word quickly becomes metaphorical: the rock designates God Himself, His solidity, His reliability. David constantly uses it: "O Lord! To You I cry. My rock!" (Psalms 28:1). In Deuteronomy, Moses reminds the people that God is "the rock who gave birth to you" (Deuteronomy 32:18), establishing a link between the physical protection of the rock and the divine protection of the Creator God.
H6697H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites us to seek in God a stability inaccessible to the storms of life. When the Bible says that God is a rock, it affirms that trust in Him rests on something permanent, unlike human supports that collapse. It is an invitation to build one's life, prayer, and faith on the unshakeable foundation of God, especially in times of trouble or doubt. This image of the rock also reinforces meditation on God's faithfulness: just as the rock nourished Israel in the desert, God sustains today those who trust in Him.

sens: Midianite prince during the Exodus
Father of Cozbi
H6698G.detail:
1. Tsur is a Midianite prince, one of the five leaders of the Midianite peoples mentioned during the events at Sinai. He is the father of Cozbi, a Midianite woman who seduced a man of Israel and was killed along with him by Phinehas for leading Israel into idolatry (Numbers 25:15).
2. The name Tsur literally means "rock" in Hebrew, an image of strength and stability; this meaning reveals the character of the father, leader of a powerful Midianite house.
H6698G.origine: Tsur comes from the Hebrew root צוּר (tsur), which means "rock" or "stone." This root evokes solidity and strength. The same word is used in the Bible to refer to the rock struck by Moses in the desert, and God Himself is often called the "Rock" of Israel. Here, the name of Cozbi's father carries the sense of strength and power, which is fitting for a Midianite clan leader.
H6698G.emploi: Tsur appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 25:15, in the account of the events at Peor. It is there that we learn that Cozbi, the woman killed by Phinehas, was his daughter and that he was the chief of a Midianite household. His role in the text is limited to this genealogical mention, but it recalls the importance of the scandal at Peor, where a Midianite prince used his connections to seduce the people of Israel.

sens: Midianite prince, father of Cozbi
One of the five Midianite leaders killed during the conquest
Son of Jehiel and chief of Gibeon
H6698H.detail:
1. Tsur was a Midianite prince and the father of Cozbi. He is mentioned as one of the five kings or leaders of Midian who were killed when the Israelites defeated Midian after Balaam had advocated for the seduction of the Israelites (Numbers 31:8).
2. Tsur is among the five Midianite princes — Evi, Rekem, Tsur, Hur, and Reba — who were under Sihon, king of the Amorites, and lived in the land at the time of the Israelite conquest (Joshua 13:21). These leaders all perished in battle.
3. Another Tsur, son of Jehiel, was the father or chief of Gibeon; he represents a different lineage, unrelated to the Midianite prince.
H6698H.origine: The name Tsur means "rock" in Hebrew. This name evokes solidity and stability, qualities expected of a leader or prince. Like many biblical names, it describes a physical or moral reality — here the strength and firmness of a rock.
H6698H.emploi: Two individuals bear this name in the provided biblical usages. The first, Tsur the Midianite, is mentioned twice: in Numbers 31:8, where he is designated as one of the five kings of Midian killed during Israel's victory, and in Joshua 13:21, which repeats this account and confirms his status as a prince under Sihon. The second, Tsur son of Jehiel, is associated with Gibeon; he appears in other passages not provided here. The two mentions of the Midianite underscore the importance of his defeat in the history of the conquest.
H6698H.portee: The mention of Tsur reminds us that God gave victory to Israel over peoples who opposed Him. His elimination, along with his four fellow princes, shows how the Lord judged those who led the Israelites into sin and idolatry.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the united monarchy
Son of Abiel and father of the brothers listed among the descendants of Benjamin
H6698I.detail: 1. Tsur is a Benjaminite mentioned in the genealogies from the time when Israel was united under one king. He appears in the list of descendants of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles 8:30, presented as the son of Abiel and having several brothers (Kish, Ner, Abdon, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zecher, and Mikloth). 2. The same Tsur appears again in 1 Chronicles 9:36, in a parallel genealogy. These two mentions confirm that he is an ancient figure from the tribe of Benjamin, recorded in Israel's genealogical memory.
H6698I.origine: The name Tsur means "rock" in Hebrew. It is a symbolic name, referring to stability and strength, like many Hebrew personal names that evoke qualities or images of protection. This type of name was common among families in the Old Testament to express the hope or values that parents wished to convey.
H6698I.emploi: Tsur appears only twice in the Bible, in the two parallel passages of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 8:30 and 9:36), where he is listed in the genealogy of Benjamin. These genealogical lists, which trace back to the time of the united monarchy or earlier, position Tsur as a link in the genealogical chain of the people of Israel. His name appears among other important ancestors of the tribe, notably his brother Kish, who would be the father of King Saul.

sens: The visible appearance of a thing, its outer form
The plan, the diagram, the graphic representation of a construction
The arrangement of a building, its structure and organization
H6699.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the visible and recognizable aspect of a thing — its silhouette, its configuration. It is what one sees when looking at something.
2. It can also mean the plan or drawing that one traces for construction, the master plan that one follows. In Ezekiel 43:11, the prophet must show Israel "the form of this house, its arrangement… all its drawings": these are the detailed plans of the future temple, as an architect would draw them.
3. More broadly, it refers to the overall arrangement, the structure of a building — how it is organized, where its entrances, rooms, and elements are located.
H6699.origine: The Hebrew word צוּרָה (tsurah) comes from a root that means "to form, to shape." It is related to other words in the same family that evoke the formation or tracing of a line. The initial image is that of giving shape to something by drawing or shaping it — like an artisan tracing the contours of a work before realizing it.
H6699.emploi: This word appears very rarely in the Hebrew Bible (mainly in Ezekiel). In Ezekiel 43:11, it designates the drawings, plans, and arrangement of the restored temple that the prophet must describe to the Israelites. The context is that of the reconstruction of the temple: they need to see the plan (the drawing), the overall configuration (the form), and all the concrete arrangements (exits, entrances, ordinances) in order to execute them faithfully. The word is thus used in an architectural and technical register, to speak of the visible shaping of a divine project.
H6699.portee: This word reminds us that God gives His people a clear vision of what He wants them to accomplish. The drawing of the temple is not an ornament or a fancy: it is a precise plan that God entrusts to Ezekiel so that the Israelites can understand and obey. This speaks to us of clarity and order in God's designs — He does not ask for vague things, but reveals His will in a concrete and intelligible manner.
